You're one of twenty-one soldiers in a tiny stone outpost. Coming up the hill are ten thousand men.
It's 1897, on India's northwest frontier. Your post, Saragarhi, is just a signal tower between two British forts.
Your job is to pass messages, with flashes of sunlight from a mirror.
One morning, the hills turn black with tribesmen. Your signalman flashes to the fort. We're under attack.
The reply comes back. Help can't get through. So your sergeant, Ishar Singh, decides you won't surrender.
For hours, twenty-one rifles hold back an entire army. Charge after charge breaks against your walls.
Then, hidden by smoke, they break through a wall.
One by one, your friends fall. And through all of it, the signalman keeps flashing every detail to the fort.
His last message asks for permission to put down the mirror, and pick up his rifle.
All twenty-one die at their posts. Not one of them surrenders.
Back then, Indian soldiers couldn't receive Britain's highest medal. So all twenty-one got the highest award they were allowed. And every twelfth of September, India's army still remembers them.
